extracted.intended_audience: agency staff, policymakers, and public commenters engaged in federal rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing effective public comments on federal rulemakings, emphasizing contributions to substantive regulatory quality and to procedural legitimacy, plus recommendations on timing, outreach, and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive quality contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should add information, analysis, or perspective that improves the rule's likely effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Task Force frames comments as serving substantive quality; effective comments supply evidence or analysis the agency lacks, identify unintended consequences, offer alternative regulatory text, or provide implementation expertise from regulated entities or beneficiaries. Focus is on information that meaningfully informs the agency's decision about regulatory design and likely effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide empirical evidence the agency lacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply empirical evidence that fills gaps in the agency's record or analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical evidence is singled out as a key form of substantive contribution. Commenters should bring new data, studies, or empirical analysis that the docket does not already contain and that materially informs regulatory choices. Place detailed data/technical analyses in appendices if needed (see plain language guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify unintended consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight potential unintended consequences of the proposed rule that the agency may not have considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pointing out plausible adverse side-effects or operational outcomes helps agencies anticipate and mitigate harms. Where possible, explain mechanisms and provide evidence or examples demonstrating those consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose alternative regulatory text
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer specific alternative regulatory language or concrete drafting suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing alternate text or concrete edits is more actionable than general objections. Agencies value ready-to-use regulatory text because it lowers the cost of adopting changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide implementation expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring practical knowledge from regulated entities or beneficiaries about how rules would operate in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments that convey implementation experience (e.g., operational constraints, compliance realities, administrative burdens) improve rule design. Such expertise can include examples, case studies, or operational metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural legitimacy contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should reflect the breadth of affected interests to enhance the rulemaking's procedural legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Task Force emphasizes that beyond technical quality, comments confer legitimacy when they demonstrate representation across affected constituencies. Agencies should be able to see that a range of interests—especially those not normally heard—are engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent or articulate an under-represented constituency
rubrics_metrics.description: Make explicit when a comment represents an under-represented constituency and explain who is being represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Task Force assigns special legitimacy weight to comments from under-represented constituencies; commenters should state clearly whom they speak for and why that perspective is distinct. This helps agencies assess the breadth of affected interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage at the earliest practical stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Participate in rulemaking at ANPRM or pre-proposal stages, use petitions for rulemaking, or request direct stakeholder meetings during rule development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments submitted earlier (ANPRM/pre-proposal) are more impactful. The Task Force recommends earlier engagement including petitions for rulemaking and direct stakeholder meetings during development because they allow stakeholders to shape regulatory alternatives before positions harden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even-handed outreach and diversity of commenters
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage comments from outside the usual stakeholder coalitions and seek geographic and demographic diversity among commenters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should conduct even-handed outreach to broaden participation. For commenters, building coalitions across diverse constituencies and ensuring geographic/demographic diversity strengthens collective influence and procedural legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain language and structured presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Write comments in plain language readable by agency staff who are not subject-matter experts; place key requested changes up front and technical detail in appendices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key requested changes should appear in the first paragraph or an executive summary. Technical detail belongs in appendices to keep the main comment accessible. This increases the likelihood agency staff will grasp and act on the comment's main points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coalition-building across diverse constituencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Form or join coalitions that span different kinds of stakeholders to signal broader legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coalition-building across diverse constituencies demonstrates breadth of affected interests and can amplify influence. The Task Force highlights that cross-sector or cross-demographic coalitions are particularly persuasive to agencies seeking to gauge public impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serve both substantive quality and procedural legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for comments that simultaneously improve the rule's technical quality and demonstrate representative breadth of concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Task Force's underlying frame is that effective comments should serve both functions: supply actionable, evidence-based input while also showing that a diversity of affected interests has been heard. Comments that do both are especially valuable to agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use petitions and direct meetings as underused engagement tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider petitions for rulemaking and direct stakeholder meetings as additional avenues to influence rule development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Task Force notes petitions for rulemaking are underused and that direct meetings during rule development can add weight to stakeholder positions. These tools can be alternatives or complements to written docket comments, especially for early-stage influence.
